188: | `MCP_URL`            | `https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp`  | The MCP endpoint URL to probe.           |
189: | `MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER`   | `https://cal.hajnal.space`       | The configured authorization-server issuer. |
190: | `MCP_REDIRECT`       | `http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback` | The admitted loopback redirect URI.      |
191: | `MCP_TIMEOUT_MS`     | `15000`                          | Request timeout in milliseconds.         |
192: | `MCP_RECORD_DIR`     | OS temp directory                | Where the deterministic record is written. |
193: 
194: Exit codes: `0` all assertions pass; `1` one or more assertions fail (the
195: intentional Phase 0.4 baseline against the current production component);
196: `2` harness error. The deterministic record is written to
197: `$MCP_RECORD_DIR/mcp-acceptance-security-isolation.json`.
198: 
199: ## Requirements
200: 
201: - Node.js 18 or newer (global `fetch`). CI uses Node 22.
202: - No third-party dependencies. The harness uses only Node built-ins.
203: 
204: ## Invocation
205: 
206: Run the focused command from the repository root:
207: 
208: ```sh
209: node mcp-acceptance/harness.js
210: ```
211: 
212: By default this targets the production endpoint
213: (`https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp`). To target a production-equivalent deployment
214: or a local instance, set `MCP_URL`:
215: 
216: ```sh
217: # Target a production-equivalent deployment (e.g. a staging ingress)
218: MCP_URL=https://staging.example.com/mcp node mcp-acceptance/harness.js
219: 
220: # Target a locally running production component (same mcp-server binary)
221: MCP_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3001/mcp node mcp-acceptance/harness.js
222: ```
223: 
224: ### Configuration (environment variables)
225: 
226: | Variable               | Default                          | Description                                  |
227: | ---------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
228: | `MCP_URL`              | `https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp`  | The MCP endpoint URL to probe.               |
229: | `MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSION` | `2025-03-26`                     | The `protocolVersion` to negotiate.          |
230: | `MCP_CLIENT_NAME`      | `commoncal-mcp-acceptance`       | `clientInfo.name` in the initialize request. |
231: | `MCP_CLIENT_VERSION`   | `0.1.0`                          | `clientInfo.version` in the initialize req.  |
232: | `MCP_TIMEOUT_MS`       | `15000`                          | Request timeout in milliseconds.             |
233: | `MCP_RECORD_DIR`       | OS temp directory                | Where the deterministic response record is written. |
234: 
235: ### Exit codes
236: 
237: | Code | Meaning                                                        |
238: | ---- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
239: | `0`  | `initialize` is standards-compatible (PASS).                   |
240: | `1`  | `initialize` is NOT standards-compatible (FAIL) — the intentional Phase 0.1 baseline exit condition against the current production component. |
241: | `2`  | Harness error (invalid configuration, network failure, unexpected error). |
242: 
243: ### Deterministic record
244: 
245: The harness writes a deterministic record of the request and response (object
246: keys sorted, volatile headers dropped) to
247: `$MCP_RECORD_DIR/mcp-acceptance-initialize.json` (default: the OS temp
248: directory). The path is printed on every run.
249: 
250: ## CI usage
251: 
252: In CI, point the harness at a production-equivalent deployment and treat a
253: non-zero exit as a real failure once the production component is fixed. During
254: Phase 0 the harness is expected to be red; record the failure as the baseline.
255: 
256: ```sh
257: # Example CI step (production-equivalent deployment)
258: MCP_URL=https://staging.example.com/mcp \
259:   MCP_RECORD_DIR="$RUNNER_TEMP/mcp-acceptance" \
260:   node mcp-acceptance/harness.js
261: ```
262: 
263: ## Verification (harness self-test)
264: 
265: A verification-only mock server exercises both the PASS and FAIL paths without
266: touching production. It is not a release artifact.
267: 
268: ```sh
269: # Start the mock server in one terminal
270: node mcp-acceptance/mock/server.js
271: 
272: # In another terminal:
273: # FAIL path — mock mirrors the CURRENT production behavior (expect exit 1)
274: MCP_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3999/mcp-current node mcp-acceptance/harness.js
275: echo "exit: $?"   # -> 1
276: 
277: # PASS path — mock returns a standards-compatible initialize (expect exit 0)
278: MCP_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3999/mcp-compliant node mcp-acceptance/harness.js
279: echo "exit: $?"   # -> 0
280: ```
281: 
282: Self-contained verifiers (they start and clean up the mock server themselves):
283: 
284: ```sh
285: # Phase 0.1 harness: both exit paths (default mock port 3999)
286: node mcp-acceptance/verify.js
287: 
288: # Phase 0.2 discovery harness: both exit paths with focused A1/A2/A4
289: # violations on the FAIL path and a passing A3 (default mock port 3998,
290: # issuer host 3999; use --port to avoid collisions)
291: node mcp-acceptance/verify-discovery.js
292: 
293: # Phase 0.3 oauth-lifecycle harness: both exit paths (default mock port 4001,
294: # issuer host 4002; use --port to avoid collisions)
295: node mcp-acceptance/verify-oauth-lifecycle.js
296: 
297: # Phase 0.4 security-isolation harness: both exit paths (default mock port
298: # 4003, issuer host 4004; use --port to avoid collisions)
299: node mcp-acceptance/verify-security-isolation.js
300: ```
301: 
302: The Phase 0.1/0.2 mock (`mock/server.js`) mirrors production's two-host
303: topology: the MCP host (MOCK_PORT) serves the MCP endpoint and the
304: protected-resource metadata; the issuer host (MOCK_ISSUER_PORT, default
305: MOCK_PORT + 1) serves the authorization-server metadata (SPA HTML in the
306: current mode, valid JSON in the compliant mode).
307: 
308: The Phase 0.3/0.4 mock (`mock/lifecycle-server.js`) is driven by a single
309: world selector (`MOCK_WORLD`, default `compliant`; `current` mirrors
310: production today). In the compliant world it implements the full OAuth + MCP
311: lifecycle (DCR, Authorization Code + S256 PKCE, token exchange, JWKS, and the
312: authenticated MCP lifecycle) plus verification-only test hooks (`/_test/*`)
313: for driving the negative token and grant-state cases. In the current world it
314: mirrors the verified current production state (the authorization service is
315: not deployed; the MCP gateway does not implement the MCP lifecycle).
316: 
317: ## Files
318: 
319: - `harness.js` — the Phase 0.1 standalone black-box harness (initialize
320:   standards-compliance).
321: - `discovery.js` — the Phase 0.2 standalone black-box harness (public 401
322:   challenge + protected-resource and authorization-server metadata discovery).
323: - `oauth-lifecycle.js` — the Phase 0.3 standalone black-box harness (DCR,
324:   Authorization Code + S256 PKCE, token exchange, and the authenticated MCP
325:   lifecycle through `calendar_list`).
326: - `security-isolation.js` — the Phase 0.4 standalone black-box harness
327:   (fail-closed token/grant cases and concurrent-identity isolation).
328: - `lib.js` — shared helpers for the Phase 0.3/0.4 harnesses (OAuth flow, MCP
329:   calls, JWT helpers, deterministic JSON).
330: - `fixtures/initialize-request.json` — the `initialize` request fixture (reused
331:   from the slice1-lab request shape; owned by this harness).
332: - `verify.js` — self-contained verification of both Phase 0.1 harness exit
333:   paths.
334: - `verify-discovery.js` — self-contained verification of both Phase 0.2
335:   harness exit paths, including the focused A1/A2/A4 violations and the
336:   passing A3 on the FAIL path.
337: - `verify-oauth-lifecycle.js` — self-contained verification of both Phase 0.3
338:   harness exit paths.
339: - `verify-security-isolation.js` — self-contained verification of both Phase
340:   0.4 harness exit paths.
341: - `mock/server.js` — verification-only mock server for Phase 0.1/0.2 (PASS +
342:   FAIL fixtures, two-host topology).
343: - `mock/lifecycle-server.js` — verification-only mock server for Phase 0.3/0.4
344:   (full OAuth + MCP lifecycle, world selector, test hooks).
345: - `mock/oauth-provider.js` — verification-only mock OAuth provider (DCR,
346:   Authorization Code + S256 PKCE, token exchange, JWKS, token validation,
347:   grants, token minting).
348: - `README.md` — this document.

#!/usr/bin/env sh
set -eu

# Tests for the MCP database backup/restore contract (slice 9):
#   - mcp_image_contains_sqlite_cli
#   - backup_snapshot_passes_integrity_check
#   - deployment_docs_name_mcp_backup_restore_and_verification_steps

repo_root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
work_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$work_dir"' EXIT

PASSED=0
FAILED=0

pass() {
  echo "PASS: $1"
  PASSED=$((PASSED + 1))
}

fail() {
  echo "FAIL: $1" >&2
  FAILED=$((FAILED + 1))
}

# --- mcp_image_contains_sqlite_cli -----------------------------------------
# The documented online backup command (sqlite3 ... VACUUM INTO) must be

# the Dockerfile installs the CLI; the runtime image is debian:bookworm-slim
# with no other sqlite3 source.
if grep -Eq 'apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends[[:space:]].*\bsqlite3\b' \

  pass "mcp_image_contains_sqlite_cli"
else
  fail "mcp_image_contains_sqlite_cli: Dockerfile.mcp must install the sqlite3 CLI"
fi

# The documented backup procedure (VACUUM INTO on a live WAL database) must
# produce a consistent, readable SQLite file.
if ! command -v sqlite3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "SKIP: backup_snapshot_passes_integrity_check (sqlite3 CLI not installed)"
else
  live_db="$work_dir/mcp-server.db"
  snapshot="$work_dir/mcp-server-backup.db"

  sqlite3 "$live_db" "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;" >/dev/null
  sqlite3 "$live_db" \

  sqlite3 "$live_db" "VACUUM INTO '$snapshot';"

  rows=$(sqlite3 "$snapshot" "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mcp_audit;")
  request=$(sqlite3 "$snapshot" "SELECT request_id FROM mcp_audit;")

47: ## Slice 2 evidence (2026-08-30)
48: 
49: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`), now driving a **real** CommonCal
50: service (`slice1-lab/src/bin/commoncal.rs`, axum on :4002) instead of the Slice 1
51: auto-approving fake. The CommonCal service owns a session, a consent page, an
52: `mcp_grant` store, and calendar data; it talks to the auth server over a
53: loopback private API (`:4001/internal/interactions/:handoff`, bearer-keyed) to
54: look up and decide handoffs. Result: **25 PASS / 0 FAIL** (Slice 1's 20 proofs
55: still green + 5 new Slice 2 proofs).
56: 
57: - S2-1 approve → MCP `calendar_list` returns the user's **real** calendars
58:   (Work + Personal), not a hardcoded value — passes.
59: - S2-2 deny → `access_denied`, **no** grant created — passes.
60: - S2-3 grant ownership: `grant.user_id` = the logged-in subject,
61:   `grant.client_id` = the DCR client — passes.
62: - S2-4 scope intersection: grant records the requested ∩ catalog set; the
63:   unknown `evil` scope is dropped, all nine catalog scopes kept — passes.
64: - S2-5 immediate revocation: revoking the grant makes an otherwise-valid JWT
65:   fail at the MCP layer (grant check is per-request, not just at token issue) — passes.
66: 
67: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 2)
68: 
69: 1. **Grant scopes come from the auth server, not CommonCal.** CommonCal has no
70:    copy of the scope catalog, so it cannot compute the requested ∩ catalog
71:    intersection itself. The auth server now returns `grantedScopes` (the
72:    intersection) in the handoff view, and CommonCal records those on the grant
73:    (falling back to the raw requested set only for views that predate the field).
74:    This keeps the grant and the JWT in agreement. If the catalog ever moves or
75:    CommonCal gains its own catalog, this handoff field can be dropped.
76: 2. **`localhost` vs `127.0.0.1` cookie domain.** The login sets the CommonCal
77:    session cookie for the `127.0.0.1` host; the auth server's consent redirect
78:    must therefore target `127.0.0.1:4002` (not `localhost:4002`) or the browser/
79:    client drops the cookie on a different domain and loops on login. The auth
80:    server's `COMMONCAL` default is pinned to `127.0.0.1` for this reason.
81: 3. **Login client must not follow redirects.** The CommonCal login responds
82:    `303 → /`; a redirect-following client then GETs `/` (no such route) and sees
83:    a 404 that masks the real login status. The harness uses a no-redirect client
84:    for login and a redirect-following client for the consent chain, sharing one
85:    `Arc<Jar>` cookie store.
86: 4. **Grant-first ordering.** CommonCal writes the `mcp_grant` *before* deciding
87:    consent with the auth server. If the decide step fails, the grant still
88:    exists (safe: the user can revoke it); the alternative (consent-first) would
89:    leave a granted-but-unrecorded state. This is a deliberate, documented choice.
90: 
91: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 1)
92: 
93: 1. **`prompt=consent` is required to keep `offline_access`.** `oidc-provider`'s
94:    `check_scope.js` strips `offline_access` unless the authorization request's
95:    `prompt` includes `consent` (the condition `PARAM_LIST.has('prompt') &&
96:    !prompts.has('consent')` is always evaluated because `PARAM_LIST` is the full
97:    valid-parameter list). The harness therefore always sends `prompt=consent`.
98:    This is a non-obvious provider behavior; re-verify if the provider is upgraded.
99: 2. **OIDC vs resource scope split.** The `scopes` config holds only OIDC scopes
100:    (`openid`, `offline_access`); the nine CommonCal catalog scopes are declared on
101:    the resource server (`getResourceServerInfo().scope`). Putting catalog scopes in
102:    `scopes` made the provider treat them as OIDC scopes and loop on consent. The
103:    client `scope` allow-list is omitted from DCR (the provider validates it against
104:    OIDC scopes only). Correct per the provider model, but subtle.
105: 3. **Fake CommonCal always approves.** Slice 1 is allowed one hardcoded approval;
106:    the :4002 interaction host auto-approves login+consent. Slice 2 replaces this
107:    with a real authenticated CommonCal session.
108: 4. **P8 ordering.** The provider's refresh-token reuse detection invalidates the
109:    whole chain once an old token is replayed, so the harness verifies the rotated
110:    token is usable *before* replaying the old one.

112: ## Slice 3 evidence (2026-08-31)
113: 
114: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 3 adds **login continuation**
115: (magic-link + open-redirect guard), **consent recovery** (expiry, replay,
116: idempotent retry, duplicate-grant, scope-replace, cross-user, stale membership),
117: and **grant management** (authenticated list / narrow-update / no-broaden /
118: revoke) to the real CommonCal service. Result: **37 PASS / 0 FAIL** (Slice 1's
119: 20 + Slice 2's 5 + 12 new Slice 3 proofs).
120: 
121: - S3-1 magic-link login: request → single-use token → verify sets session and
122:   303s to the bound same-origin `continue`; continuation then completes consent — passes.
123: - S3-2 open-redirect guard: `http://`, `//`, `https://`, `/\` continues all fall
124:   back to same-origin `/` — passes.
125: - S3-3 no forged identity: user2's approval writes a grant owned by user2 (id=2)
126:   allowing user2's calendar; user1 has no grant for that client — passes.
127: - S3-4 expired handoff rejected on render (502) — passes.
128: - S3-5 handoff replay: first consent consumes it, second rejected — passes.
129: - S3-6 idempotent retry: bridge decide fails *after* the grant write; retry
130:   succeeds; the grant is not broadened or duplicated — passes.
131: - S3-7 duplicate-grant: two approvals yield exactly one active grant (replace,
132:   not accumulate) — passes.
133: - S3-8 no stale membership: a removed calendar is absent from MCP results even
134:   though the grant still listed it (live membership intersected at read time) — passes.
135: - S3-9 no scope union: a narrow re-approval *replaces* the grant's scopes (9 → 1),
136:   it does not union them — passes.
137: - S3-10 no cross-user access: user2 cannot revoke or list user1's grant — passes.
138: - S3-11 grant management: list shows the grant; narrow update ok; broaden denied
139:   (403); revoke ok; re-revoke 404 — passes.
140: 
141: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 3)
142: 
143: 1. **The bridge test hook fires only on `consent` decisions.** The login decision
144:    precedes the grant write, so a generic "fail the next decide" hook would
145:    disrupt login, not the grant-first/bridge-second ordering under test. The hook
146:    is therefore scoped to `kind == "consent"`. This is a lab-only test seam; the
147:    production path has no such hook.
148: 2. **Login and consent are separate handoffs.** The provider issues a *login*
149:    handoff first; deciding it resumes to a *new consent* handoff. The idempotent
150:    retry proof therefore resolves the login handoff to the consent handoff once,
151:    then retries the *consent* decision. Reusing the login handoff for the retry
152:    would 404 (already consumed). This separation is a provider-model property, not
153:    a lab artifact.
154: 3. **Grant management is session-scoped and ownership-checked.** `GET /grants`,
155:    `PATCH /grants/:id`, and `DELETE /grants/:id` all require a CommonCal session
156:    and reject grants not owned by that user (404, to avoid revealing existence).
157:    Update is narrow-only (every requested calendar must already be allowed), so a
158:    user cannot broaden a grant outside the original consent.
159: 4. **Magic-link tokens are `Uuid::v4` and single-use.** The request endpoint is
160:    anti-enumeration (same response whether or not the account exists) and the
161:    `continue` is sanitized by the shared open-redirect guard. The link is returned
162:    to the caller only because this is a loopback lab; a real service would deliver
163:    it out-of-band.
164: 
165: ### Risk / follow-up (not fixed in this slice)
166: 
167: - **Harness does not fail-fast on a port conflict.** If a stale `commoncal` /
168:   `mcp-echo` / auth-server process from a killed run still holds a loopback port,
169:   the freshly spawned process exits on bind but the health check hits the stale
170:   process, so proofs silently run against old code. This cost real debugging time.
171:   Recommended follow-up: after spawning each child, verify the process is still
172:   alive (and the port is owned by the new PID) and fail fast otherwise. Out of
173:   scope for Slice 3 (harness robustness, not a slice feature).

175: ## Slice 4 evidence (2026-08-31)
176: 
177: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 4 adds **authorization protocol
178: hardening** (DCR rate limiting, size limits, audit logging, callback-shape policy
179: framework, key overlap, exact token lifetimes) and **storage hardening** (PostgreSQL
180: adapter cleanup, structured redaction) to the auth server. Result: **47 PASS / 0 FAIL**
181: (Slice 1's 20 + Slice 2's 5 + Slice 3's 12 + 10 new Slice 4 proof assertions).
182: 
183: - S4-1 PostgreSQL adapter cleanup: expired `provider_entity` row inserted via test
184:   hook is purged by `POST /internal/cleanup` — passes.
185: - S4-2 DCR rate limiting: 4th DCR request in a window of 3 rejected with 429 — passes.
186: - S4-3 DCR size limit: oversized payload (>16KB) rejected with 413 — passes.
187: - S4-4 DCR audit logging: DCR attempt recorded in the audit log (`dcr_attempt`
188:   event) — passes.
189: - S4-5 callback-shape policy: custom-scheme redirect rejected, exact-HTTPS redirect
190:   rejected, loopback redirect admitted by the policy framework — passes (3).
191: - S4-6 key overlap: JWKS has 2 keys with distinct kids; token signed with kid A
192:   is accepted against the 2-key JWKS (key lookup by kid) — passes.
193: - S4-7 exact token lifetimes: access token TTL is exactly 300s (`exp - iat = 300`) — passes.
194: - S4-8 structured redaction: bridge key in `client_name` is masked as `[REDACTED]`
195:   in the audit log — passes.

197: ### Implementation notes (Slice 4)
198: 
199: - **DCR rate limiting** is a per-IP sliding window (default 10 req/60s, configurable
200:   via `POST /internal/test/dcr-rate-limit`). The counter is in-memory (lab-appropriate);
201:   production would use a shared store.
202: - **DCR size limit** is a 16KB cap on the JSON body, enforced before parsing.
203: - **DCR audit logging** records `dcr_attempt` events (IP, client_name, redirect_uris,
204:   grant_types) in a bounded in-memory ring buffer (1000 entries). Readable via
205:   `GET /internal/audit`.
206: - **Callback-shape policy** (`dcr-policy.mjs`) is a declarative framework: each policy
207:   entry has a `scheme`, `host`, `port`, and `path` constraint. The lab config admits
208:   only the loopback redirect. Adding a production callback is a config change, not a
209:   code change.
210: - **Second JWKS key** (`slice4-test-rs256-b`) is a distinct RSA-256 key published
211:   alongside the primary (`slice1-test-rs256`). The provider signs with the primary;
212:   the resource server validates by kid lookup, proving multi-key JWKS works.
213: - **Structured redaction** (`redact()` in `server.mjs`) masks the bridge key value
214:   in all log and audit output. Applied to `client_name`, `redirect_uris`, and
215:   `grant_types` fields in audit entries.
216: - **PostgreSQL adapter cleanup** adds a `cleanup()` method to the `PostgresAdapter`
217:   that deletes expired `provider_entity` rows (where `expires_at < now()`).
218:   Exposed via `POST /internal/cleanup`.
219: 
220: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 4)
221: 
222: 1. **Rate limiting is per-IP, in-memory.** The lab uses the client IP (always
223:    `127.0.0.1` in loopback) as the rate-limit key. In production behind a proxy,
224:    the `X-Forwarded-For` header would need to be trusted. The in-memory store is
225:    lab-appropriate; production would use Redis or a similar shared store.
226: 2. **Audit log is in-memory, bounded.** The 1000-entry ring buffer is sufficient
227:    for the lab. Production would ship to a durable store (e.g., the same PostgreSQL
228:    instance) with retention policy.
229: 3. **The second JWKS key is never used for signing.** It exists only to prove the
230:    resource server can look up the correct key by kid from a multi-key JWKS. In
231:    production, key rotation would involve signing with the new key and publishing
232:    both keys until old tokens expire.

286: ## Slice 6 evidence (2026-09-01)
287: 
288: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 6 adds **complete read
289: capability** to the MCP connector: `availability_find`, `event_get`, and
290: `event_search` tools with typed parameter schemas, grant-based scope and
291: calendar enforcement, range validation, and access-level filtering.
292: Result: **54 PASS / 0 FAIL** (prior 47 + 7 new Slice 6 proofs).
293: 
294: - S6-1 `availability_find` returns real availability slots (busy + free) for
295:   seeded events — passes.
296: - S6-2 `event_get` returns full event details (title, description, location,
297:   access=full) — passes.
298: - S6-3 `event_search` returns real events (Team Standup + Design Review) in
299:   range — passes.
300: - S6-4 scope enforcement: token without `commoncal.availability.read` →
301:   `availability_find` denied — passes.
302: - S6-5 calendar access: `event_get` for calendar 999 (not in grant) → denied — passes.
303: - S6-6 range validation: range > 31 days → rejected — passes.
304: - S6-7 access level: `event_get` with basic scope only → description + location
305:   stripped, access=basic — passes.
306: 
307: ### Implementation notes (Slice 6)
308: 
309: - **Typed parameter schemas** use `#[derive(JsonSchema)]` structs at module level
310:   (required by the `rmcp` `#[tool]` macro). Each tool declares its parameters
311:   via `Parameters<T>` for compile-time schema generation.
312: - **Grant-based enforcement** is per-request: each tool call loads the active
313:   grant from CommonCal's internal API, checks scopes and calendar membership,
314:   then proxies to the resource endpoint. Revocation takes effect immediately.
315: - **Access-level filtering** (basic vs full) strips `description` and `location`
316:   from event responses when the grant lacks `commoncal.event.read.details`.
317:   The `access` field in the response tells the client which level was applied.
318: - **Range validation** enforces `to > from` and `range <= 31 days` on all
319:   time-range tools. Timestamps accept both Unix epoch seconds and RFC 3339.
320: - **CommonCal internal endpoints** (`/internal/availability`, `/internal/event`,
321:   `/internal/events`) are bridge-key authenticated and return structured JSON.
322:   The MCP echo server proxies to these endpoints, applying grant checks before
323:   the call.
324: 
325: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 6)
326: 
327: 1. **Grant lookup is per-request, not cached.** Each tool call fetches the
328:    active grant from CommonCal. This ensures immediate revocation but adds a
329:    round-trip per call. In production, a short TTL cache (e.g., 30s) could
330:    reduce latency while keeping revocation near-instant.
331: 2. **Access-level filtering is response-side, not query-side.** The MCP echo
332:    server fetches the full event and strips fields client-side. An alternative
333:    would be a `?fields=basic` query parameter on the CommonCal endpoint. The
334:    current approach is simpler and keeps the CommonCal API uniform.
335: 3. **`availability_find` accepts multiple calendar IDs.** The tool iterates
336:    over each calendar and aggregates slots. This matches the production
337:    `availability_find` signature but means a single bad calendar ID fails the
338:    entire call. An alternative would be per-calendar error reporting.

47: ## Slice 2 evidence (2026-08-30)
48: 
49: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`), now driving a **real** CommonCal
50: service (`slice1-lab/src/bin/commoncal.rs`, axum on :4002) instead of the Slice 1
51: auto-approving fake. The CommonCal service owns a session, a consent page, an
52: `mcp_grant` store, and calendar data; it talks to the auth server over a
53: loopback private API (`:4001/internal/interactions/:handoff`, bearer-keyed) to
54: look up and decide handoffs. Result: **25 PASS / 0 FAIL** (Slice 1's 20 proofs
55: still green + 5 new Slice 2 proofs).
56: 
57: - S2-1 approve → MCP `calendar_list` returns the user's **real** calendars
58:   (Work + Personal), not a hardcoded value — passes.
59: - S2-2 deny → `access_denied`, **no** grant created — passes.
60: - S2-3 grant ownership: `grant.user_id` = the logged-in subject,
61:   `grant.client_id` = the DCR client — passes.
62: - S2-4 scope intersection: grant records the requested ∩ catalog set; the
63:   unknown `evil` scope is dropped, all nine catalog scopes kept — passes.
64: - S2-5 immediate revocation: revoking the grant makes an otherwise-valid JWT
65:   fail at the MCP layer (grant check is per-request, not just at token issue) — passes.
66: 
67: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 2)
68: 
69: 1. **Grant scopes come from the auth server, not CommonCal.** CommonCal has no
70:    copy of the scope catalog, so it cannot compute the requested ∩ catalog
71:    intersection itself. The auth server now returns `grantedScopes` (the
72:    intersection) in the handoff view, and CommonCal records those on the grant
73:    (falling back to the raw requested set only for views that predate the field).
74:    This keeps the grant and the JWT in agreement. If the catalog ever moves or
75:    CommonCal gains its own catalog, this handoff field can be dropped.
76: 2. **`localhost` vs `127.0.0.1` cookie domain.** The login sets the CommonCal
77:    session cookie for the `127.0.0.1` host; the auth server's consent redirect
78:    must therefore target `127.0.0.1:4002` (not `localhost:4002`) or the browser/
79:    client drops the cookie on a different domain and loops on login. The auth
80:    server's `COMMONCAL` default is pinned to `127.0.0.1` for this reason.
81: 3. **Login client must not follow redirects.** The CommonCal login responds
82:    `303 → /`; a redirect-following client then GETs `/` (no such route) and sees
83:    a 404 that masks the real login status. The harness uses a no-redirect client
84:    for login and a redirect-following client for the consent chain, sharing one
85:    `Arc<Jar>` cookie store.
86: 4. **Grant-first ordering.** CommonCal writes the `mcp_grant` *before* deciding
87:    consent with the auth server. If the decide step fails, the grant still
88:    exists (safe: the user can revoke it); the alternative (consent-first) would
89:    leave a granted-but-unrecorded state. This is a deliberate, documented choice.
90: 
91: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 1)
92: 
93: 1. **`prompt=consent` is required to keep `offline_access`.** `oidc-provider`'s
94:    `check_scope.js` strips `offline_access` unless the authorization request's
95:    `prompt` includes `consent` (the condition `PARAM_LIST.has('prompt') &&
96:    !prompts.has('consent')` is always evaluated because `PARAM_LIST` is the full
97:    valid-parameter list). The harness therefore always sends `prompt=consent`.
98:    This is a non-obvious provider behavior; re-verify if the provider is upgraded.
99: 2. **OIDC vs resource scope split.** The `scopes` config holds only OIDC scopes
100:    (`openid`, `offline_access`); the nine CommonCal catalog scopes are declared on
101:    the resource server (`getResourceServerInfo().scope`). Putting catalog scopes in
102:    `scopes` made the provider treat them as OIDC scopes and loop on consent. The
103:    client `scope` allow-list is omitted from DCR (the provider validates it against
104:    OIDC scopes only). Correct per the provider model, but subtle.
105: 3. **Fake CommonCal always approves.** Slice 1 is allowed one hardcoded approval;
106:    the :4002 interaction host auto-approves login+consent. Slice 2 replaces this
107:    with a real authenticated CommonCal session.
108: 4. **P8 ordering.** The provider's refresh-token reuse detection invalidates the
109:    whole chain once an old token is replayed, so the harness verifies the rotated
110:    token is usable *before* replaying the old one.

112: ## Slice 3 evidence (2026-08-31)
113: 
114: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 3 adds **login continuation**
115: (magic-link + open-redirect guard), **consent recovery** (expiry, replay,
116: idempotent retry, duplicate-grant, scope-replace, cross-user, stale membership),
117: and **grant management** (authenticated list / narrow-update / no-broaden /
118: revoke) to the real CommonCal service. Result: **37 PASS / 0 FAIL** (Slice 1's
119: 20 + Slice 2's 5 + 12 new Slice 3 proofs).
120: 
121: - S3-1 magic-link login: request → single-use token → verify sets session and
122:   303s to the bound same-origin `continue`; continuation then completes consent — passes.
123: - S3-2 open-redirect guard: `http://`, `//`, `https://`, `/\` continues all fall
124:   back to same-origin `/` — passes.
125: - S3-3 no forged identity: user2's approval writes a grant owned by user2 (id=2)
126:   allowing user2's calendar; user1 has no grant for that client — passes.
127: - S3-4 expired handoff rejected on render (502) — passes.
128: - S3-5 handoff replay: first consent consumes it, second rejected — passes.
129: - S3-6 idempotent retry: bridge decide fails *after* the grant write; retry
130:   succeeds; the grant is not broadened or duplicated — passes.
131: - S3-7 duplicate-grant: two approvals yield exactly one active grant (replace,
132:   not accumulate) — passes.
133: - S3-8 no stale membership: a removed calendar is absent from MCP results even
134:   though the grant still listed it (live membership intersected at read time) — passes.
135: - S3-9 no scope union: a narrow re-approval *replaces* the grant's scopes (9 → 1),
136:   it does not union them — passes.
137: - S3-10 no cross-user access: user2 cannot revoke or list user1's grant — passes.
138: - S3-11 grant management: list shows the grant; narrow update ok; broaden denied
139:   (403); revoke ok; re-revoke 404 — passes.
140: 
141: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 3)
142: 
143: 1. **The bridge test hook fires only on `consent` decisions.** The login decision
144:    precedes the grant write, so a generic "fail the next decide" hook would
145:    disrupt login, not the grant-first/bridge-second ordering under test. The hook
146:    is therefore scoped to `kind == "consent"`. This is a lab-only test seam; the
147:    production path has no such hook.
148: 2. **Login and consent are separate handoffs.** The provider issues a *login*
149:    handoff first; deciding it resumes to a *new consent* handoff. The idempotent
150:    retry proof therefore resolves the login handoff to the consent handoff once,
151:    then retries the *consent* decision. Reusing the login handoff for the retry
152:    would 404 (already consumed). This separation is a provider-model property, not
153:    a lab artifact.
154: 3. **Grant management is session-scoped and ownership-checked.** `GET /grants`,
155:    `PATCH /grants/:id`, and `DELETE /grants/:id` all require a CommonCal session
156:    and reject grants not owned by that user (404, to avoid revealing existence).
157:    Update is narrow-only (every requested calendar must already be allowed), so a
158:    user cannot broaden a grant outside the original consent.
159: 4. **Magic-link tokens are `Uuid::v4` and single-use.** The request endpoint is
160:    anti-enumeration (same response whether or not the account exists) and the
161:    `continue` is sanitized by the shared open-redirect guard. The link is returned
162:    to the caller only because this is a loopback lab; a real service would deliver
163:    it out-of-band.
164: 
165: ### Risk / follow-up (not fixed in this slice)
166: 
167: - **Harness does not fail-fast on a port conflict.** If a stale `commoncal` /
168:   `mcp-echo` / auth-server process from a killed run still holds a loopback port,
169:   the freshly spawned process exits on bind but the health check hits the stale
170:   process, so proofs silently run against old code. This cost real debugging time.
171:   Recommended follow-up: after spawning each child, verify the process is still
172:   alive (and the port is owned by the new PID) and fail fast otherwise. Out of
173:   scope for Slice 3 (harness robustness, not a slice feature).

175: ## Slice 4 evidence (2026-08-31)
176: 
177: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 4 adds **authorization protocol
178: hardening** (DCR rate limiting, size limits, audit logging, callback-shape policy
179: framework, key overlap, exact token lifetimes) and **storage hardening** (PostgreSQL
180: adapter cleanup, structured redaction) to the auth server. Result: **47 PASS / 0 FAIL**
181: (Slice 1's 20 + Slice 2's 5 + Slice 3's 12 + 10 new Slice 4 proof assertions).
182: 
183: - S4-1 PostgreSQL adapter cleanup: expired `provider_entity` row inserted via test
184:   hook is purged by `POST /internal/cleanup` — passes.
185: - S4-2 DCR rate limiting: 4th DCR request in a window of 3 rejected with 429 — passes.
186: - S4-3 DCR size limit: oversized payload (>16KB) rejected with 413 — passes.
187: - S4-4 DCR audit logging: DCR attempt recorded in the audit log (`dcr_attempt`
188:   event) — passes.
189: - S4-5 callback-shape policy: custom-scheme redirect rejected, exact-HTTPS redirect
190:   rejected, loopback redirect admitted by the policy framework — passes (3).
191: - S4-6 key overlap: JWKS has 2 keys with distinct kids; token signed with kid A
192:   is accepted against the 2-key JWKS (key lookup by kid) — passes.
193: - S4-7 exact token lifetimes: access token TTL is exactly 300s (`exp - iat = 300`) — passes.
194: - S4-8 structured redaction: bridge key in `client_name` is masked as `[REDACTED]`
195:   in the audit log — passes.
196: 
197: ### Implementation notes (Slice 4)
198: 
199: - **DCR rate limiting** is a per-IP sliding window (default 10 req/60s, configurable
200:   via `POST /internal/test/dcr-rate-limit`). The counter is in-memory (lab-appropriate);
201:   production would use a shared store.
202: - **DCR size limit** is a 16KB cap on the JSON body, enforced before parsing.
203: - **DCR audit logging** records `dcr_attempt` events (IP, client_name, redirect_uris,
204:   grant_types) in a bounded in-memory ring buffer (1000 entries). Readable via
205:   `GET /internal/audit`.
206: - **Callback-shape policy** (`dcr-policy.mjs`) is a declarative framework: each policy
207:   entry has a `scheme`, `host`, `port`, and `path` constraint. The lab config admits
208:   only the loopback redirect. Adding a production callback is a config change, not a
209:   code change.
210: - **Second JWKS key** (`slice4-test-rs256-b`) is a distinct RSA-256 key published
211:   alongside the primary (`slice1-test-rs256`). The provider signs with the primary;
212:   the resource server validates by kid lookup, proving multi-key JWKS works.
213: - **Structured redaction** (`redact()` in `server.mjs`) masks the bridge key value
214:   in all log and audit output. Applied to `client_name`, `redirect_uris`, and
215:   `grant_types` fields in audit entries.
216: - **PostgreSQL adapter cleanup** adds a `cleanup()` method to the `PostgresAdapter`
217:   that deletes expired `provider_entity` rows (where `expires_at < now()`).
218:   Exposed via `POST /internal/cleanup`.
219: 
220: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 4)
221: 
222: 1. **Rate limiting is per-IP, in-memory.** The lab uses the client IP (always
223:    `127.0.0.1` in loopback) as the rate-limit key. In production behind a proxy,
224:    the `X-Forwarded-For` header would need to be trusted. The in-memory store is
225:    lab-appropriate; production would use Redis or a similar shared store.
226: 2. **Audit log is in-memory, bounded.** The 1000-entry ring buffer is sufficient
227:    for the lab. Production would ship to a durable store (e.g., the same PostgreSQL
228:    instance) with retention policy.
229: 3. **The second JWKS key is never used for signing.** It exists only to prove the
230:    resource server can look up the correct key by kid from a multi-key JWKS. In
231:    production, key rotation would involve signing with the new key and publishing
232:    both keys until old tokens expire.

286: ## Slice 6 evidence (2026-09-01)
287: 
288: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 6 adds **complete read
289: capability** to the MCP connector: `availability_find`, `event_get`, and
290: `event_search` tools with typed parameter schemas, grant-based scope and
291: calendar enforcement, range validation, and access-level filtering.
292: Result: **54 PASS / 0 FAIL** (prior 47 + 7 new Slice 6 proofs).
293: 
294: - S6-1 `availability_find` returns real availability slots (busy + free) for
295:   seeded events — passes.
296: - S6-2 `event_get` returns full event details (title, description, location,
297:   access=full) — passes.
298: - S6-3 `event_search` returns real events (Team Standup + Design Review) in
299:   range — passes.
300: - S6-4 scope enforcement: token without `commoncal.availability.read` →
301:   `availability_find` denied — passes.
302: - S6-5 calendar access: `event_get` for calendar 999 (not in grant) → denied — passes.
303: - S6-6 range validation: range > 31 days → rejected — passes.
304: - S6-7 access level: `event_get` with basic scope only → description + location
305:   stripped, access=basic — passes.
306: 
307: ### Implementation notes (Slice 6)
308: 
309: - **Typed parameter schemas** use `#[derive(JsonSchema)]` structs at module level
310:   (required by the `rmcp` `#[tool]` macro). Each tool declares its parameters
311:   via `Parameters<T>` for compile-time schema generation.
312: - **Grant-based enforcement** is per-request: each tool call loads the active
313:   grant from CommonCal's internal API, checks scopes and calendar membership,
314:   then proxies to the resource endpoint. Revocation takes effect immediately.
315: - **Access-level filtering** (basic vs full) strips `description` and `location`
316:   from event responses when the grant lacks `commoncal.event.read.details`.
317:   The `access` field in the response tells the client which level was applied.
318: - **Range validation** enforces `to > from` and `range <= 31 days` on all
319:   time-range tools. Timestamps accept both Unix epoch seconds and RFC 3339.
320: - **CommonCal internal endpoints** (`/internal/availability`, `/internal/event`,
321:   `/internal/events`) are bridge-key authenticated and return structured JSON.
322:   The MCP echo server proxies to these endpoints, applying grant checks before
323:   the call.
324: 
325: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 6)
326: 
327: 1. **Grant lookup is per-request, not cached.** Each tool call fetches the
328:    active grant from CommonCal. This ensures immediate revocation but adds a
329:    round-trip per call. In production, a short TTL cache (e.g., 30s) could
330:    reduce latency while keeping revocation near-instant.
331: 2. **Access-level filtering is response-side, not query-side.** The MCP echo
332:    server fetches the full event and strips fields client-side. An alternative
333:    would be a `?fields=basic` query parameter on the CommonCal endpoint. The
334:    current approach is simpler and keeps the CommonCal API uniform.
335: 3. **`availability_find` accepts multiple calendar IDs.** The tool iterates
336:    over each calendar and aggregates slots. This matches the production
337:    `availability_find` signature but means a single bad calendar ID fails the
338:    entire call. An alternative would be per-calendar error reporting.
339: 
340: ## Slice 7 evidence (2026-09-01)
341: 
342: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 7 adds **ordinary mutations**
343: to the MCP connector: `event_create`, `event_update`, and `reminder_set` tools
344: with typed parameter schemas, grant-based scope and calendar enforcement,
345: optimistic concurrency (version check), idempotency keys, and per-request
346: grant checks. Result: **60 PASS / 0 FAIL** (prior 54 + 6 new Slice 7 proofs).
347: 
348: - S7-1 `event_create` returns a new event with id, title, version=1 — passes.
349: - S7-2 `event_update` with correct `expected_version` succeeds, version increments to 2 — passes.
350: - S7-3 `reminder_set` returns a reminder with id and offset_minutes — passes.
351: - S7-4 scope enforcement: token without `commoncal.event.create` → `event_create` denied — passes.
352: - S7-5 idempotency: same `idempotency_key` returns the same event with `replayed=true` — passes.
353: - S7-6 stale-conflict: `event_update` with wrong `expected_version` → `version_conflict` error — passes.
354: 
355: ### Implementation notes (Slice 7)
356: 
357: - **`event_create`** accepts `calendar_id`, `title`, optional `description`/`location`,
358:   `start_utc`/`end_utc` (ISO 8601 or epoch), and optional `idempotency_key`.
359:   The CommonCal internal endpoint (`POST /internal/event`) creates the event with
360:   `version=1` and records the idempotency key for safe retries.
361: - **`event_update`** requires `expected_version` for optimistic concurrency.
362:   The CommonCal internal endpoint (`PATCH /internal/event/:id`) checks the version
363:   and returns 409 on mismatch. The MCP tool translates this to a
364:   `version_conflict` error message.
365: - **`reminder_set`** accepts `calendar_id`, `event_id`, and `offset_minutes`.
366:   The CommonCal internal endpoint (`POST /internal/reminder`) creates the reminder
367:   and returns its id.
368: - **Scope enforcement** is per-request: `event_create` requires
369:   `commoncal.event.create`, `event_update` requires `commoncal.event.update`,
370:   and `reminder_set` requires `commoncal.reminder.write`. Calendar membership
371:   is also checked against the grant's `allowed_calendar_ids`.
372: - **Idempotency** is key-based: the first call creates the event and stores the
373:   key→event_id mapping; subsequent calls with the same key return the existing
374:   event with `replayed=true`.
375: 
376: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 7)
377: 
378: 1. **Idempotency keys are stored in-memory (lab-only).** The key→event_id map
379:    lives in the CommonCal process memory. In production, this would need a
380:    durable store (e.g., the same PostgreSQL instance) with a TTL. The lab
381:    approach is sufficient for proving the protocol behavior.
382: 2. **`event_update` uses full-replace semantics for provided fields.** Omitted
383:    fields keep their current value; provided fields replace the old value. This
384:    matches the "partial update" pattern but means a client cannot clear a field
385:    (e.g., set `description` to null) without a dedicated "clear" mechanism.
386:    The production API may need explicit null semantics.
387: 3. **`reminder_set` does not check for duplicate reminders.** Setting the same

# Slices 13–14: client delivery evidence (2026-10-18)

The operator requested implementing slices 13 and 14 together, explicitly
allowing work despite stale prerequisite status. README delivery therefore
proceeds with visible verification limits rather than declaring release support.
No production deployment, issuer change, real-account consent or grant revocation
was performed. SQLite remains the authoritative hosting decision.

## Reconciliation

Inspected both the happening repository's manifests/results and the
plan-orchestrator source and read-only orchestration database. The database
marks tasks 12 and 13 completed, but its linked QA results explicitly preserve
the live matrix hold. Slice 13's manifest records an operator completion override
on 2026-10-17 and says the live OAuth/calendar lifecycle remains unverified.
No newer passing live client matrix was found. Administrative completion is not
proof of an authenticated calendar read.

The old production fix plan is superseded by `docs/AUTH-PRODUCTION.md` and
`docs/MCP-PRODUCTION-SUCCESSFUL-COMMANDS-2026-10-09.md`. Their deployment and
protocol evidence does not establish released-client lifecycle compatibility.

## New implementation

- README is the canonical setup surface for OpenCode, Codex and Claude Code,
  with prerequisites, consent meaning, verification, local removal, server-side
  revocation, troubleshooting, version limits and official references.
- OpenCode v2 configuration is `mcp.servers.commoncal`, not the v1 flat map.
  Its temporary-disable flag is `disabled`, not `enabled`.
- `mcp-acceptance/client-snippets.js` executes the marked README shell snippets
  in isolated temporary client profiles, substitutes only a loopback fixture
  URL, compares the README JSON with CLI-generated OpenCode config, attempts
  callback observation, and checks removal. No production credentials are read
  or copied. The loopback registration fixture deliberately rejects DCR after
  recording public client metadata, before any browser opens or token is issued.
- Actual OpenCode v2.0.20 DCR used
  `http://127.0.0.1:55740/callback` (later run: port 55777), public auth method
  `none`. Thus the old `/mcp/oauth/callback` policy did not match it. A failing
  regression test reproduced that rejection before the policy change.
- Production config adds only the observed HTTP IPv4 loopback `/callback` shape,
  and only if IPv4 loopback is already permitted by configuration. Existing
  configured callback shapes remain. No arbitrary HTTPS callback is admitted.

## Verification results

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `node --check mcp-acceptance/client-snippets.js` | PASS |
| `node --test test/*.test.mjs` in `slice1-lab/auth-server` | PASS, 8 tests |
| `node tests/production-integration.mjs` in `slice1-lab/auth-server` | PASS, including actual provider DCR for `/callback`, existing OAuth/PKCE, bridge, restart, backup/restore, refresh/replay/revocation, key overlap, audit and rate limits |
| `node mcp-acceptance/client-snippets.js codex` | PASS, add/list/remove and absence after removal |
| `node mcp-acceptance/client-snippets.js opencode` | FAIL overall; add, README JSON agreement and observed callback PASS; list/logout checks FAIL |
| `node mcp-acceptance/client-snippets.js claude` | NOT RUN: executable unavailable (`spawn claude ENOENT`); runner exits 1 |

The regression negatives cover HTTPS, localhost, IPv6, absent/privileged ports,
wrong/trailing-slash paths, query/fragment, credentials and external hosts for the
new callback shape. Disabling IPv4 in the configured allowlist disables it too.
The configured legacy callback tests remain green.

Root cause **confirmed**: LibreSSL 3.3.6 (macOS default) does **not** support `openssl verify -verify_hostname` or `openssl x509 -checkhost` — both are OpenSSL-specific flags. The command exits 1 with a usage error, which `auth-tls.sh` interprets as "certificate does not cover auth.hajnal.space." This is an **environment limitation, not a code defect** (the script is correct for OpenSSL, which is what production uses).

Let me confirm the test file's failures all trace to this, and run the remaining Helm/Flux + SQLite suites in parallel:

299: 
300: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 6 adds **complete read
301: capability** to the MCP connector: `availability_find`, `event_get`, and
302: `event_search` tools with typed parameter schemas, grant-based scope and
303: calendar enforcement, range validation, and access-level filtering.
304: Result: **54 PASS / 0 FAIL** (prior 47 + 7 new Slice 6 proofs).
305: 
306: - S6-1 `availability_find` returns real availability slots (busy + free) for
307:   seeded events — passes.
308: - S6-2 `event_get` returns full event details (title, description, location,
309:   access=full) — passes.
310: - S6-3 `event_search` returns real events (Team Standup + Design Review) in
311:   range — passes.
312: - S6-4 scope enforcement: token without `commoncal.availability.read` →
313:   `availability_find` denied — passes.
314: - S6-5 calendar access: `event_get` for calendar 999 (not in grant) → denied — passes.
315: - S6-6 range validation: range > 31 days → rejected — passes.
316: - S6-7 access level: `event_get` with basic scope only → description + location
317:   stripped, access=basic — passes.
318: 
319: ### Implementation notes (Slice 6)
320: 
321: - **Typed parameter schemas** use `#[derive(JsonSchema)]` structs at module level
322:   (required by the `rmcp` `#[tool]` macro). Each tool declares its parameters
323:   via `Parameters<T>` for compile-time schema generation.
324: - **Grant-based enforcement** is per-request: each tool call loads the active
325:   grant from CommonCal's internal API, checks scopes and calendar membership,
326:   then proxies to the resource endpoint. Revocation takes effect immediately.
327: - **Access-level filtering** (basic vs full) strips `description` and `location`
328:   from event responses when the grant lacks `commoncal.event.read.details`.
329:   The `access` field in the response tells the client which level was applied.
330: - **Range validation** enforces `to > from` and `range <= 31 days` on all
331:   time-range tools. Timestamps accept both Unix epoch seconds and RFC 3339.
332: - **CommonCal internal endpoints** (`/internal/availability`, `/internal/event`,
333:   `/internal/events`) are bridge-key authenticated and return structured JSON.
334:   The MCP echo server proxies to these endpoints, applying grant checks before
335:   the call.
336: 
337: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 6)
338: 
339: 1. **Grant lookup is per-request, not cached.** Each tool call fetches the
340:    active grant from CommonCal. This ensures immediate revocation but adds a
341:    round-trip per call. In production, a short TTL cache (e.g., 30s) could
342:    reduce latency while keeping revocation near-instant.
343: 2. **Access-level filtering is response-side, not query-side.** The MCP echo
344:    server fetches the full event and strips fields client-side. An alternative
345:    would be a `?fields=basic` query parameter on the CommonCal endpoint. The
346:    current approach is simpler and keeps the CommonCal API uniform.
347: 3. **`availability_find` accepts multiple calendar IDs.** The tool iterates
348:    over each calendar and aggregates slots. This matches the production
349:    `availability_find` signature but means a single bad calendar ID fails the
350:    entire call. An alternative would be per-calendar error reporting.

353: 
354: Same harness (`slice1-lab/` → `lab-prove`). Slice 7 adds **ordinary mutations**
355: to the MCP connector: `event_create`, `event_update`, and `reminder_set` tools
356: with typed parameter schemas, grant-based scope and calendar enforcement,
357: optimistic concurrency (version check), idempotency keys, and per-request
358: grant checks. Result: **60 PASS / 0 FAIL** (prior 54 + 6 new Slice 7 proofs).
359: 
360: - S7-1 `event_create` returns a new event with id, title, version=1 — passes.
361: - S7-2 `event_update` with correct `expected_version` succeeds, version increments to 2 — passes.
362: - S7-3 `reminder_set` returns a reminder with id and offset_minutes — passes.
363: - S7-4 scope enforcement: token without `commoncal.event.create` → `event_create` denied — passes.
364: - S7-5 idempotency: same `idempotency_key` returns the same event with `replayed=true` — passes.
365: - S7-6 stale-conflict: `event_update` with wrong `expected_version` → `version_conflict` error — passes.
366: 
367: ### Implementation notes (Slice 7)
368: 
369: - **`event_create`** accepts `calendar_id`, `title`, optional `description`/`location`,
370:   `start_utc`/`end_utc` (ISO 8601 or epoch), and optional `idempotency_key`.
371:   The CommonCal internal endpoint (`POST /internal/event`) creates the event with
372:   `version=1` and records the idempotency key for safe retries.
373: - **`event_update`** requires `expected_version` for optimistic concurrency.
374:   The CommonCal internal endpoint (`PATCH /internal/event/:id`) checks the version
375:   and returns 409 on mismatch. The MCP tool translates this to a
376:   `version_conflict` error message.
377: - **`reminder_set`** accepts `calendar_id`, `event_id`, and `offset_minutes`.
378:   The CommonCal internal endpoint (`POST /internal/reminder`) creates the reminder
379:   and returns its id.
380: - **Scope enforcement** is per-request: `event_create` requires
381:   `commoncal.event.create`, `event_update` requires `commoncal.event.update`,
382:   and `reminder_set` requires `commoncal.reminder.write`. Calendar membership
383:   is also checked against the grant's `allowed_calendar_ids`.
384: - **Idempotency** is key-based: the first call creates the event and stores the
385:   key→event_id mapping; subsequent calls with the same key return the existing
386:   event with `replayed=true`.
387: 
388: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 7)
389: 
390: 1. **Idempotency keys are stored in-memory (lab-only).** The key→event_id map
391:    lives in the CommonCal process memory. In production, this would need a
392:    durable store (e.g., the same PostgreSQL instance) with a TTL. The lab
393:    approach is sufficient for proving the protocol behavior.
394: 2. **`event_update` uses full-replace semantics for provided fields.** Omitted
395:    fields keep their current value; provided fields replace the old value. This
396:    matches the "partial update" pattern but means a client cannot clear a field
397:    (e.g., set `description` to null) without a dedicated "clear" mechanism.
398:    The production API may need explicit null semantics.
399: 3. **`reminder_set` does not check for duplicate reminders.** Setting the same
400:    `offset_minutes` on the same event twice creates two reminders. A production
401:     system would likely enforce uniqueness on (event_id, offset_minutes).

501: ### Implementation notes (Slice 9)
502: 
503: - **Origin enforcement was the one outstanding gap.** `transport.rs::server_config()`
504:   previously set only `with_allowed_hosts([host])`; rmcp's `allowed_origins`
505:   defaulted to empty, which disables `Origin` validation entirely. It now sets
506:   `with_allowed_origins([origin])` where `origin = url.origin().ascii_serialization()`
507:   (e.g. `https://mcal.hajnal.space`). Per rmcp semantics, a non-empty
508:   `allowed_origins` list means requests carrying an `Origin` header must match
509:   (RFC 6454 scheme/host/port), while requests without an `Origin` header still
510:   pass - so CLI/non-browser clients are unaffected and cross-origin browser
511:   requests are blocked.
512: - **Rate limiting is per-identity, in-memory.** The fixed-window limiter is keyed
513:   by `user_id:client_id` (resolved after authentication, before grant lookup).
514:   Configurable via `MCP_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 60), `MCP_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS`
515:   (default 60), and `MCP_RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED`. Denial returns JSON-RPC code `-2004`
516:   with the safe message "rate limit exceeded".
517: - **Provider outage is safe by construction.** `TokenError::InvalidToken(String)`
518:   is mapped in `auth.rs::token_error_params` to the static pair
519:   `("invalid_token", "invalid authorization token")`; the internal detail is only
520:   logged via `tracing::warn!` and never returned to the client.
521: 
522: ### Least-confident decisions (Slice 9)
523: 
524: 1. **Origin = the resource URL's own origin (same-origin only).** The allowed
525:    origin is derived from the MCP resource URL, so only same-origin browser
526:    requests are admitted. If a cross-origin web client must call the MCP endpoint,
527:    its origin must be added to the allow-list (a config change, not a code change).
528:    This is the most restrictive, safest default.
529: 2. **rmcp's port-matching is lenient.** `origin_is_allowed` treats an allowed
530:    origin with no explicit port as matching any port on that host. This is rmcp's
531:    defined behavior, not something this slice overrides; the security property
532:    that matters (blocking different-host / different-scheme origins) holds.
533: 3. **Rate limiter is in-memory.** Sufficient for a single-instance resource
534:    server. A multi-instance deployment would need a shared store (e.g. the same
535:    SQLite/PostgreSQL instance) to enforce a global window.

551: - Gate 4 is approved. Implement only Slice 1, then stop for review; preserve and assess the existing `slice1-lab/` and `mcp-server/Cargo.toml` partial evidence/work before changing it.
552: - Target assistant applications are Codex, Claude, and OpenCode.

554: - Required later deliverable: update `README.md` with commands verified against released Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode clients; do not edit it before compatibility slices pass.

38: ## Slice 1 evidence (2026-08-29)
39: 
40: Proof harness: `slice1-lab/` → `cargo run -p slice1-lab --bin lab-prove` (spawns the
41: `oidc-provider` 9.12.0 auth server on :4000, a fake CommonCal interaction host on
42: :4002, and the `rmcp`-backed `mcp-echo` on :3001; PostgreSQL persistence on :55432).
43: Result: **20 PASS / 0 FAIL**.
44: 
45: - P1 strict DCR public client (no empty optional fields) — passes.
46: - P2 wildcard / malformed / arbitrary-HTTPS redirect all rejected — passes (3).
47: - P3 S256 PKCE + exact loopback redirect — passes.
48: - P4 JWT claims `sub`/`aud`=resource/`scope`/`jti`/`ttl<=600s`/`amr` — passes.
49: - P5 consent scope intersection drops the unknown `evil` scope — passes.
50: - P6 authenticated MCP `initialize` → `tools/list` → `tools/call calendar_list` — passes (3).
51: - P7 unauthenticated 401+WWW-Authenticate, one-time code, missing verifier, wrong
52:   audience, different-resource exchange all rejected — passes (5).
53: - P8 refresh rotation + new-token usable + old-token replay rejected — passes (3).
54: - P9 RFC 7009 revocation then refresh rejected — passes.
55: - P10 provider state survives an auth-server restart (PostgreSQL) — passes.
56: 
57: All seven Slice 1 mandatory stop conditions are satisfied; no translation proxy added.
